items.title: The English Channel is not getting narrower
items.claim: Is the English Channel closing as Britain and France converge?

options.text: Yes, by about 1 cm per year
No — there is no convergent plate boundary; both sit on the Eurasian plate. The Channel was carved by megaflood erosion around 450,000 and 160,000 years ago
Yes, by about 1 metre per year
It widens by 10 cm per year

items.reveal:
Britain was connected to mainland Europe as recently as 8,000 years ago (the Doggerland landscape). The Channel itself was formed by catastrophic megafloods when a glacial lake in the southern North Sea breached a chalk ridge at Dover-Calais (Gupta et al., Nature 2007).

Both Britain and France sit on the Eurasian plate, with no relative motion at this scale. The 'closing' or 'opening' claim is geophysically wrong.

Isostatic rebound is causing northern Britain to rise and southern England to sink — relative sea level rises faster on the south coast.
items.why: Plausible-sounding numerical claims about geographic change can be entirely fictional. The right test is mechanism, not vivid number — there's no plate boundary to drive Channel closure.

items.title: Glaciers can move metres per day during surges

options.text: Typically tens to hundreds of metres per year for valley glaciers; outlet glaciers like Jakobshavn (Greenland) reached around 17 km/year (around 46 m/day) in 2012; surge-type glaciers (around 1% of all glaciers) can move metres per day for months
Always 1 mm per year, too slow to detect
All glaciers move at the same uniform rate

items.reveal:
Glacier flow combines internal deformation (creep — ice flowing under its own weight, around 10-100 m/year for valley glaciers) and basal sliding (much faster when meltwater lubricates the bed).

Jakobshavn Isbrae drains around 7% of the Greenland Ice Sheet; its mass loss has been measured by satellite altimetry and GRACE. Variegated Glacier (Alaska) surged at around 65 m/day in 1982-83.

Climate warming has accelerated many outlet glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica — ice shelves at the front buttress the ice behind; when shelves break up, the ice behind speeds up. Pine Island and Thwaites (Antarctica) are the major current concerns.
items.why: Glacier dynamics control sea-level contribution. Flow speeds and acceleration mechanisms are central uncertainties in projecting 21st-century sea-level rise.
